The available records support a proposed lease-termination effort at SSA locations, with facility types and dates varying across the list. They do not support the original claim that about 600 of roughly 1,200 field offices were closed. The sources reviewed also do not establish that every lease cancellation occurred or quantify resulting service loss, delays, or harm to claimants. corrected_proposal.title: HUD Terminates Fair-Housing Grants; Evidence Does Not Show an Office-Wide Shutdown
corrected_proposal.description_short: A court filing describes HUD's immediate termination of 78 FHIP grants in February 2025, not a shutdown of all fair-housing enforcement.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: A March 13, 2025 federal court filing describes HUD notices terminating 78 active Fair Housing Initiatives Program grants effective February 27. The filing quotes the notices’ stated reason and says no further explanation was provided. This supports a targeted grant action affecting nonprofit fair-housing work. The sources reviewed do not establish that HUD ended every proactive investigation, zeroed out FHEO’s budget, or disabled all federal enforcement.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On February 27, 2025, the Department of Housing and Urban Development terminated 78 active Fair Housing Initiatives Program (FHIP) grants. A March 13 federal court filing by fair-housing organizations describes form notices making the terminations effective immediately and quotes the notice as saying the awards no longer effectuated program goals or agency priorities. The filing says the notices attributed the decision to presidential direction under the order establishing the Department of Government Efficiency. Those statements document the notices as quoted in the plaintiffs’ filing; the filing is not a judicial finding that the action was unlawful. The supported scope is the specified FHIP awards and their nonprofit recipients. The evidence reviewed does not establish that HUD ended all proactive fair-housing investigations, zeroed out the Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity budget, or stopped every form of federal enforcement. Claims about staffing reductions and downstream service losses require their own evidence and are not asserted here. The card therefore records the narrower documented grant action, distinguishes the court challenge from a court ruling, and leaves the broader office-wide claims unresolved.

corrected_proposal.title: Trump’s FY2026 Budget Proposed Replacing Housing Choice Vouchers With State Grants
corrected_proposal.description_short: The FY2026 budget proposed replacing federal voucher-account funding with state rental assistance; Congress later funded Housing Choice Vouchers for 2026.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: HUD’s detailed FY2026 budget justification, available beginning May 30, 2025, proposed no funding for Tenant-Based Rental Assistance, which includes Housing Choice Vouchers, and requested a new State Rental Assistance Program. The Congressional Research Service described the state grant as intended to replace federal rental-assistance programs. This was a budget proposal, not an April 2025 cancellation of new vouchers; Congress enacted 2026 voucher funding on February 3, 2026.
corrected_proposal.description_long:
HUD’s detailed FY2026 budget request, made available beginning May 30, 2025, proposed no funding for Tenant-Based Rental Assistance (TBRA), the federal account that includes Housing Choice Vouchers, and requested a new state-run State Rental Assistance Program. The Congressional Research Service described the design as eliminating federal rental-assistance programs, including Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers, and replacing them with a state block grant. HUD’s budget materials describe TBRA as the account serving about 2.3 million families in 2025.

This supports a corrected entry about a proposed federal funding redesign, not the frozen claim that the administration announced an April 2025 stop to new vouchers. The budget materials do not show that applicants were removed from waiting lists, existing vouchers were rescinded, homelessness increased, or tens of thousands of households lost assistance; those consequences should not be asserted here. Nor was the proposal enacted as a voucher shutdown: HUD later reported that the Consolidated Appropriations Act signed February 3, 2026 provided funding for the Housing Choice Voucher program. Keep the entry centered on what the administration proposed, distinguish the proposal from the later enacted funding, and leave actual household effects unclaimed.

corrected_proposal.description_short: Trump Used “Animals” Remark During May 2018 California Immigration Roundtable
corrected_proposal.description_medium: At a May 16, 2018, White House roundtable on sanctuary-city policies, President Donald Trump said, “These aren’t people. These are animals” after Fresno County Sheriff Margaret Mims said she knew of an MS-13 member she could not report to ICE. corrected_proposal.description_long: On May 16, 2018, President Donald Trump held a White House roundtable with California mayors, sheriffs and other officials about sanctuary-city policies. During the discussion, Fresno County Sheriff Margaret Mims said she knew of an MS-13 member but could not tell ICE unless that person met a threshold. Trump replied that “people coming into the country” were “animals,” saying, “These aren’t people. These are animals.” In the official transcript, the remark immediately follows Mims’s reference to MS-13, but Trump’s reply does not name the gang. The White House press secretary later said Trump was referring to MS-13 gang members, and Trump said the next day that he meant MS-13. FactCheck.org reported those explanations while noting that it could not determine exactly what Trump meant in the original remark. The record should therefore describe the words and their immediate setting, then attribute the later clarification separately. It should not say the transcript proves that Trump was referring to all immigrants, or that it definitively proves he meant only MS-13. The sources establish the public remark and context; they do not document a resulting policy change or quantify harm caused by it.

The held record further alleges that Trump repeatedly favored President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan because of this business interest. The sources accessed for this repair do not establish that causal link. corrected_proposal.description_short: A February 2025 report described an ICE contractor solicitation for social-media monitoring and facial-recognition capability.

corrected_proposal.description_long: This repair narrows the frozen entry to a contractor solicitation reported by The Intercept on February 11, 2025. The article, citing contract documents, says ICE planned to monitor and locate negative social-media discussion about the agency and senior officials. It also quotes a request for facial-recognition capability that could use a subject’s photograph to search the internet for associated information. Those details support a proposal for online monitoring and identity research. They do not establish that a system was awarded, deployed, or used to identify undocumented immigrants across multiple platforms. The source also does not establish that ICE selected political dissenters as targets; it describes monitoring discussion of ICE and its leadership and frames the procurement around threats to personnel and facilities. The original card’s claims of a live mass-identification program, database matching, and disproportionate targeting are therefore removed. This is a serious privacy and speech concern at the proposal stage, with implementation and actual effects unresolved.

corrected_proposal.title: Trump Order Calls for Immigration Detention Pending Proceedings, Subject to Law
corrected_proposal.description_short: Trump's Jan. 20 order directs detention of removable immigrants pending proceedings or removal, to the extent permitted by law.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: Section 10 of the Jan. 20, 2025 order directs DHS to use or establish detention facilities and to detain people apprehended for immigration-law violations pending removal proceedings or removal, to the extent permitted by law. That text supports a detention directive; it does not itself establish indefinite detention without charge, denied bail hearings, or immediate court blocks.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued Executive Order 14159, “Protecting the American People Against Invasion.” Section 10 directs the Homeland Security secretary to take appropriate action and use legally available resources or contracts for facilities to detain removable immigrants. It further directs detention of people apprehended for immigration-law violations while removal proceedings are pending or until removal, “to the extent permitted by law.” The order therefore supports describing a federal detention directive tied to removal proceedings and an express legal limitation. The text does not itself say that immigrants may be held indefinitely without charges, instruct immigration judges to deny bail hearings, or report that federal judges immediately blocked the order. The supplied card made those additional claims without providing a court ruling or other supporting source; they are omitted here. The order’s language alone also does not establish how long anyone was detained, how many people were affected, what agencies implemented, or how a court later ruled. This corrected entry records what the signed order says without turning its detention language into unsupported claims about custody duration, court action, or a legal finding.
